ladders.title: Master equation to constraint diagram
ladders.freq: Constraint analysis or master equation in 6 of 11 terms, 14 chair sessions
ladders.figure: A blank pair of axes: wing loading W_TO/S along the bottom, thrust loading T_SL/W_TO up the side, and the word "derive" next to it.

rungs.ask: Start from energy. Where does the master equation come from?
rungs.answer: Excess power raises the total energy: (T − D)V = W d/dt(h + V²/(2g)). Dividing by WV gives (T − D)/W = (1/V)dh/dt + (1/g)dV/dt.
rungs.say: I will start from the energy equation: excess power equals the rate of change of specific energy

rungs.ask: Now put it in sizing form, in terms of takeoff thrust and takeoff weight.
rungs.answer: Write T = αT_SL, W = βW_TO, D = qS(K₁C_L² + K₂C_L + C_D0 + C_DR) with C_L = nβW_TO/(qS), then divide by βW_TO: T_SL/W_TO = (β/α)[(qS/(βW_TO))(K₁(nβW_TO/(qS))² + K₂(nβW_TO/(qS)) + C_D0 + C_DR) + (1/V)d/dt(h + V²/(2g))].
rungs.say: I divide through by βW_TO so everything is in thrust loading and wing loading

rungs.ask: Describe every term for me.
rungs.answer: α is thrust lapse T/T_SL, β is the instantaneous weight fraction W/W_TO, q is dynamic pressure, n is load factor, K₁ and K₂ are the drag polar coefficients, C_D0 is zero-lift drag, C_DR is additional drag from stores or flaps, and the last bracket is climb plus acceleration through (1/V)dh/dt + (1/g)dV/dt.
rungs.say: α is thrust lapse and β is the weight fraction at that mission point

rungs.ask: Why those two axes?
rungs.answer: W_TO/S and T_SL/W_TO are the two design parameters the master equation depends on once a mission segment fixes q, n and the energy rate, so every segment becomes one curve in this plane; the feasible region lies above the thrust curves and left of the stall and landing lines.
rungs.say: Each mission segment becomes one boundary in the wing loading, thrust loading plane

rungs.ask: Draw the stall or landing line. Where does it come from?
rungs.answer: From V_stall = √(2βW_TO/(ρSC_Lmax)): W_TO/S ≤ ρV_stall²C_Lmax/(2β), a vertical line, with feasible designs to its left.
rungs.say: Stall fixes a maximum wing loading, a vertical line

rungs.ask: Now takeoff ground roll.
rungs.answer: With V_TO = k_TO V_stall and acceleration g αT_SL/(βW_TO), s_G = V_TO²/(2a) gives T_SL/W_TO = (β²/α) k_TO² (W_TO/S)/(ρ g C_Lmax s_G), a line rising from the origin.
rungs.say: Takeoff gives thrust loading proportional to wing loading

rungs.ask: Cruise and a sustained turn. What shape, and where is the minimum?
rungs.answer: With K₂ = 0 and constant h and V, T_SL/W_TO = (β/α)[qC_D0/(βW_TO/S) + K₁n²β(W_TO/S)/q], a bucket with its minimum at W_TO/S = (q/β)√(C_D0/K₁)/n; the turn raises the K₁ term by n².
rungs.say: The induced term carries n², and the bucket bottom is where parasite and induced drag are equal

rungs.ask: Put it on a carrier.
rungs.answer: Catapult launch replaces the takeoff roll: end speed plus wind over deck sets a minimum flying speed, which becomes a wing loading limit through C_Lmax, and the arrested landing with a low approach speed gives a strict vertical landing line further left.
rungs.say: On the carrier, catapult end speed plus wind over deck and the approach speed set the constraints

rungs.ask: Now fly it on Mars.
rungs.answer: Surface density is about 0.02 kg/m³, under 2 percent of Earth sea level, and g is 3.71 m/s², so q at a given speed is tiny and the stall line moves far left to very low wing loading; low Reynolds number and the low speed of sound add penalties, and the thrust source becomes electric propellers, which changes α.
rungs.say: Low density drives the stall line to low wing loading, and I re-derive α for an electric propeller

ladders.trap: Write the climb term as (1/V)dh/dt and the acceleration term as (1/g)dV/dt, put n² on K₁, and divide by βW_TO so every curve lands in the T_SL/W_TO versus W_TO/S plane.

ladders.title: Turbofan Brayton cycle with bypass
ladders.freq: Propulsion or Brayton in 7 of 11 terms, 15 chair sessions
ladders.figure: A two-spool turbofan sketched in side view, with a T-s diagram beside it and a request for station numbers on both.

rungs.ask: Number the stations on the engine.
rungs.answer: 0 freestream, 2 fan face, 13 fan exit in the bypass duct, 19 bypass nozzle exit, 3 compressor exit, 4 turbine inlet, 5 turbine exit, 9 core nozzle exit.
rungs.say: Station 2 is the fan face, 4 is turbine inlet, and the bypass stream is 13 to 19

rungs.ask: Which property relation do you use to draw the T-s diagram?
rungs.answer: dh = T ds + v dp, so along an isobar dT/ds = T/c_p, and constant pressure lines fan apart as temperature rises.
rungs.say: I will use dh equals T ds plus v dp

rungs.ask: Draw the ideal core cycle.
rungs.answer: 0 to 3 is isentropic compression (vertical up), 3 to 4 is constant pressure heat addition along the p₃ isobar, 4 to 9 is isentropic expansion through turbine and nozzle down to p₀, and 9 to 0 closes along the p₀ isobar as heat rejection to the atmosphere.
rungs.say: Compression and expansion are vertical, heat addition and rejection follow isobars

rungs.ask: Now add the bypass stream.
rungs.answer: The bypass air goes 0 to 13 by isentropic fan compression to a modest pressure, then 13 to 19 by expansion back to p₀, a short vertical pair that sits low on the diagram beside the core.
rungs.say: The bypass path is a separate short compression and expansion from station 0

rungs.ask: Make it real. What changes?
rungs.answer: Compression and expansion lean to the right because entropy rises with component inefficiency, and the burner shows a small total pressure drop.
rungs.say: Real components add entropy, so the vertical lines tilt right

rungs.ask: How does the turbine know how much work to make?
rungs.answer: Turbine work balances compressor plus fan work: ṁ_core(h₄ − h₅) = ṁ_core(h₃ − h₂) + ṁ_bypass(h₁₃ − h₂), and T₄ is capped by turbine materials.
rungs.say: Turbine work equals compressor work plus fan work

rungs.ask: Why do modern transports use high bypass?
rungs.answer: Thrust is F = ṁ(V_e − V₀) and propulsive efficiency is η_p = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀), so moving more mass with a smaller velocity increment produces the same thrust with less kinetic energy wasted in the jet.
rungs.say: High bypass raises propulsive efficiency by moving more mass with a smaller velocity increment

rungs.ask: Then why does a fighter use low bypass?
rungs.answer: Supersonic flight needs high specific thrust F/ṁ, which needs a high exhaust velocity, and a slim low bypass engine also keeps frontal area and wave drag small; the fan diameter, nacelle drag and ground clearance bound bypass ratio on transports too.
rungs.say: At high flight Mach the priority becomes specific thrust and frontal area

ladders.trap: Start the station numbering at 0 for freestream and 2 for the fan face, and draw the bypass stream as its own 0 to 13 to 19 path.

ladders.title: V-n diagram with altitude, weight and gusts
ladders.figure: Axes of load factor n versus airspeed, with the examiner asking for the maneuver envelope first and the gust lines later.

rungs.ask: Draw the maneuver envelope.
rungs.answer: The positive stall boundary is n = ρV²SC_Lmax/(2W), a parabola from the origin up to n_max; a horizontal line at n_max runs to dive speed V_D; the negative side uses C_Lmin up to n_min, and a vertical line at V_D closes it.
rungs.say: The left boundary is the stall parabola, the top is the structural limit

rungs.ask: Label the points.
rungs.answer: V_s is the 1 g stall speed, V_A = V_s√n_max is the corner or maneuvering speed, V_C is design cruise speed, and V_D is design dive speed.
rungs.say: The corner speed is V_s times the square root of n_max

rungs.ask: Where is this aerodynamically limited and where is it structurally limited?
rungs.answer: Left of the corner the wing reaches C_Lmax first, so the parabola is the aerodynamic limit; right of the corner the structure reaches n_max first.
rungs.say: Left of the corner the limit is aerodynamic, right of it the limit is structural

rungs.ask: Give me the stall speed at load factor n.
rungs.answer: V_stall = √(2nW/(ρSC_Lmax)), so stall speed grows with √n.
rungs.say: Stall speed carries the factor 2 and the load factor n

rungs.ask: Increase the weight. What moves?
rungs.answer: The stall parabola flattens because n = qSC_Lmax/W. With n_max fixed by the category, V_A = V_s√n_max rises with √W; if the structure is instead held to a fixed limit load n·W, the allowable n drops as 1/W and V_A stays put.
rungs.say: Heavier weight moves the corner speed right with the square root of weight

rungs.ask: Now climb to altitude.
rungs.answer: Plotted against equivalent airspeed V_e = V√(ρ/ρ₀), the aerodynamic boundaries stay put; plotted against true airspeed, the stall curves stretch right by √(ρ₀/ρ).
rungs.say: I plot in equivalent airspeed, so the aerodynamic boundaries stay fixed with altitude

rungs.ask: Add the gust lines.
rungs.answer: From n = 1 the gust lines fan out as Δn = ρ₀U_eV_e a K_g/(2W/S), with K_g = 0.88μ_g/(5.3 + μ_g) and the largest design gust at V_B, smaller at V_C and smallest at V_D.
rungs.say: Gust lines start at n equals 1 and their slope is proportional to lift curve slope over wing loading

rungs.ask: Which airplane suffers more in gusts, and why?
rungs.answer: Δn scales with a/(W/S), so a light, high aspect ratio, low wing loading airplane sees the larger gust load factor.
rungs.say: Low wing loading and high lift curve slope give the larger gust increment

ladders.trap: Use equivalent airspeed so altitude leaves the aerodynamic boundaries fixed, and write V_stall = √(2nW/(ρSC_Lmax)) with the 2 and the n.

ladders.title: Rotor power: hover to forward flight
ladders.freq: Hover momentum theory is a named signature ask of this chair
ladders.figure: A rotor disk of area A with a control volume drawn around the slipstream, later redrawn tilted in forward flight next to a power versus speed sketch.

rungs.ask: Hover. Find the induced velocity.
rungs.answer: Actuator disk momentum theory: the far wake velocity is 2v_i, so T = ṁ·2v_i = 2ρAv_i², giving v_i = √(T/(2ρA)).
rungs.say: I will use actuator disk momentum theory with a control volume around the slipstream

rungs.ask: And the ideal hover power?
rungs.say: Ideal power is T to the three halves over root 2ρA

rungs.ask: How do you measure how good a real rotor is?
rungs.answer: Figure of merit FM = P_ideal/P_actual, typically 0.7 to 0.8 for a good rotor.
rungs.say: Figure of merit compares ideal induced power with actual power

rungs.ask: What does disk loading do?
rungs.answer: Ideal power per unit thrust is √(T/A)/√(2ρ), so low disk loading gives efficient hover; a helicopter hovers efficiently and a jet lift vehicle at very high disk loading pays heavily.
rungs.say: Power per unit thrust scales with the square root of disk loading

rungs.ask: Now forward flight. Induced velocity?
rungs.answer: Glauert gives T = 2ρAv_i√(V² + v_i²); at high speed v_i ≈ T/(2ρAV), so induced power falls as 1/V.
rungs.say: Induced power falls as one over V in forward flight

rungs.ask: Sketch total power required versus speed.
rungs.answer: Total power is induced (falling as 1/V) plus profile (roughly constant, rising mildly with advance ratio) plus parasite ½ρV³f (rising as V³), a bucket shape.
rungs.say: Total power is induced plus profile plus parasite, a bucket

rungs.ask: Where do you fly for endurance and for range?
rungs.answer: Endurance is best at the bottom of the bucket, minimum power; range is best at the tangent from the origin, minimum P/V.
rungs.say: Minimum power for endurance, tangent from the origin for range

rungs.ask: Hover it on Mars.
rungs.answer: With ρ under 2 percent of Earth sea level and T = mg_Mars, hover power scales as 1/√ρ, so the vehicle needs very large, fast spinning rotors at low disk loading, and tip Mach number becomes the limit because the speed of sound is low.
rungs.say: Hover power scales with one over root ρ, so I enlarge the rotor and watch tip Mach

ladders.trap: Carry the far wake velocity as 2v_i, which gives v_i = √(T/(2ρA)) and P = T^(3/2)/√(2ρA).

ladders.title: Minimum cruise drag over span and area
ladders.freq: KKT in 8 of 11 terms; this chair asked KKT in 7 of 13 sessions
ladders.figure: Cruise drag written as a function of wing area S and span b, with a stall speed requirement and a hangar span limit listed beneath.

rungs.ask: Write the objective in S and b.
rungs.answer: With lift equal to weight, C_L = W/(qS), K = 1/(πeAR), AR = b²/S: D = qC_D0S + W²/(qπeb²).
rungs.say: Lift equals weight is an equality I use to eliminate C_L

rungs.ask: Write the constraints in standard form.
rungs.answer: Stall: g₁ = S_min − S ≤ 0 with S_min = 2W/(ρV_s²C_Lmax). Span: g₂ = b − b_max ≤ 0.
rungs.say: I write every constraint as g less than or equal to zero

rungs.ask: Before any algebra, what does each variable want?
rungs.answer: ∂D/∂S = qC_D0 > 0, so area wants to shrink to S_min; ∂D/∂b = −2W²/(qπeb³) < 0, so span wants to grow to b_max. Both constraints are active.
rungs.say: Physically, area wants to shrink and span wants to grow, so both constraints are active

rungs.ask: Prove it.
rungs.answer: KKT: ∇D + λ₁∇g₁ + λ₂∇g₂ = 0, λ ≥ 0, λᵢgᵢ = 0. The S row gives λ₁ = qC_D0, the b row gives λ₂ = 2W²/(qπeb_max³), both positive.
rungs.say: I will set up the KKT conditions

rungs.ask: Is it a minimum?
rungs.answer: Two linearly independent active constraints in two variables with strictly positive multipliers leave a critical cone of only the zero vector, so the corner is a strict local minimum.
rungs.say: With strict complementarity, the critical cone is just the origin

rungs.ask: What does λ₂ mean physically?
rungs.answer: λ₂ = −dD*/db_max, the drag saved per unit of extra allowable span, the shadow price of the hangar limit; a large λ₂ says that limit is costly.
rungs.say: The multiplier is the sensitivity of the optimal drag to the constraint limit

rungs.ask: Draw the contours and the corner.
rungs.answer: Drag contours in the (S, b) plane decrease toward small S and large b; at the corner, −∇D lies inside the cone spanned by the active constraint gradients ∇g₁ = (−1, 0) and ∇g₂ = (0, 1).
rungs.say: Minus the gradient lies in the cone of the active constraint gradients

rungs.ask: Add wing weight that grows with span. What changes?
rungs.answer: Then W depends on b, so a larger span raises induced drag through W² while lowering it through b², and an interior span optimum can appear where the span constraint goes inactive with λ₂ = 0.
rungs.say: Coupling weight to span can make the span constraint inactive

ladders.trap: Treat lift as the equality C_L = W/(qS), reason physically about each variable first, then confirm with KKT and positive multipliers.

ladders.title: One quadratic, three questions
ladders.freq: Quadratic through critical point, eigenvectors and contours is a theory chair staple; KKT in 8 of 11 terms, line search in 5 of 11
ladders.figure: f(x) = x₁² + x₁x₂ + x₂² − 3x₁ − 3x₂ written on the board, which is ½xᵀHx − bᵀx with H = [[2,1],[1,2]] and b = (3, 3).

rungs.ask: Find the critical point.
rungs.answer: ∇f = Hx − b = 0 gives x* = (1, 1), with f* = −3.
rungs.say: I set the gradient to zero, Hx equals b

rungs.ask: Classify it.
rungs.answer: H = [[2,1],[1,2]] has eigenvalues 3 and 1, both positive, so H is positive definite and x* is the strict global minimizer of this convex quadratic.
rungs.say: Both Hessian eigenvalues are positive, so this is a strict global minimum

rungs.ask: Eigenvectors, then sketch the contours.
rungs.answer: λ = 3 along (1, 1)/√2 and λ = 1 along (1, −1)/√2. Contours are ellipses centred at (1, 1) with axes at 45 degrees, long axis along (1, −1), axis ratio √3.
rungs.say: Principal axes pass through the critical point and the long axis follows the smaller eigenvalue

rungs.ask: Add x₁ + x₂ ≤ 1. Solve it.
rungs.answer: The unconstrained minimizer violates it, so the constraint is active. KKT: Hx − b + λ(1, 1) = 0 with x₁ + x₂ = 1 gives x = (½, ½), λ = 3/2 ≥ 0, f = −9/4.
rungs.say: I will set up the KKT conditions with the constraint active

rungs.ask: What does λ = 3/2 tell you?
rungs.answer: Relaxing the right-hand side from 1 to 1 + δ lowers the optimal f by about (3/2)δ, so λ is the shadow price of the constraint.
rungs.say: The multiplier is the rate of change of the optimum with the constraint limit

rungs.ask: Back to unconstrained. Start at (1, 0) and take a steepest descent step.
rungs.answer: g = (−1, −2), p = −g = (1, 2). The exact step for a quadratic is α = gᵀg/(gᵀHg) = 5/14, landing at (19/14, 5/7).
rungs.say: For a quadratic the exact step is gᵀg over gᵀHg

rungs.ask: Now do it inexactly. Does α = 1 pass Armijo?
rungs.answer: Armijo needs f(x + αp) ≤ f(x) + c₁α∇fᵀp. At α = 1, f(2, 2) = 0 sits above −2 − 5c₁, so it fails; backtracking to α = ½ gives f(1.5, 1) = −2.75, which passes.
rungs.say: I check sufficient decrease, the Armijo condition, and backtrack

rungs.ask: State strong Wolfe and check the exact step.
rungs.answer: Strong Wolfe adds |∇f(x + αp)ᵀp| ≤ c₂|∇fᵀp| with 0 < c₁ < c₂ < 1; at the exact step ∇f(x + αp)ᵀp = 0, so it satisfies the curvature condition for every c₂.
rungs.say: The curvature condition bounds the directional derivative at the new point

rungs.ask: How fast does steepest descent converge on this function?
rungs.answer: With exact line search the error in f shrinks at least by ((κ − 1)/(κ + 1))² per step, and κ = 3 gives 1/4.
rungs.say: The rate is set by the condition number, ((κ − 1)/(κ + 1)) squared

ladders.trap: Draw the contour principal axes through the critical point, with the long axis along the eigenvector of the smaller eigenvalue.

ladders.title: Surrogate from first principles
ladders.freq: Surrogates in 6 of 11 terms, asked as a 15-rung ladder
ladders.figure: Scattered sample points (xᵢ, yᵢ) for i = 1..n and a request: build me a model from these.

rungs.ask: Formulate it as an optimization problem.
rungs.answer: Choose a model linear in the parameters, ŷ(x) = Σⱼ wⱼφⱼ(x) for j = 1..m, and choose w to minimize the sum of squared errors over the samples.
rungs.say: The model is linear in the parameters, so fitting is a least squares problem

rungs.ask: Define the error and name every term with its dimension.
rungs.answer: ε(w) = Σᵢ (yᵢ − Σⱼ wⱼφⱼ(xᵢ))², with n samples, m basis functions φⱼ, weights w of size m, and Φ the n × m matrix with Φᵢⱼ = φⱼ(xᵢ).
rungs.say: Φ is n by m, rows are samples and columns are basis functions

rungs.ask: Derive the weights in summation form.
rungs.answer: ∂ε/∂w_k = −2Σᵢ φ_k(xᵢ)(yᵢ − Σⱼ wⱼφⱼ(xᵢ)) = 0, so Σⱼ (Σᵢ φ_k(xᵢ)φⱼ(xᵢ)) wⱼ = Σᵢ φ_k(xᵢ)yᵢ for each k.
rungs.say: The derivative carries a factor of 2, which cancels

rungs.ask: Stop. Same thing in vector form.
rungs.answer: ε = ‖y − Φw‖² = (y − Φw)ᵀ(y − Φw), ∇ε = −2Φᵀ(y − Φw) = 0, so ΦᵀΦw = Φᵀy, the normal equations.
rungs.say: In matrix form this is ΦᵀΦ w equals Φᵀ y

rungs.ask: When is Φ itself invertible, and what do you get?
rungs.answer: When n = m and the basis functions are independent on the samples, Φ is square and nonsingular, w = Φ⁻¹y, and the model interpolates every sample.
rungs.say: Square and full rank Φ gives interpolation

rungs.ask: More points than basis functions?
rungs.answer: n > m is overdetermined; with Φ of full column rank, w = (ΦᵀΦ)⁻¹Φᵀy is the least squares fit, which passes near the samples.
rungs.say: Overdetermined gives the least squares solution through the normal equations

rungs.ask: Fewer points than basis functions? How does the summation change?
rungs.answer: n < m is underdetermined: ΦᵀΦ is singular and infinitely many w interpolate. Pick the minimum norm one: minimize ‖w‖² subject to Φw = y, giving w = Φᵀ(ΦΦᵀ)⁻¹y, with the inner sums now over the m basis functions inside an n × n system.
rungs.say: Underdetermined, I pick the minimum norm interpolant

rungs.ask: Regularize it. Write the problem and the solution.
rungs.answer: Minimize ‖y − Φw‖² + μ‖w‖² with μ > 0, so (ΦᵀΦ + μI)w = Φᵀy and w = (ΦᵀΦ + μI)⁻¹Φᵀy; in summation form, Σⱼ (Σᵢ φ_kφⱼ + μδ_kj)wⱼ = Σᵢ φ_k yᵢ.
rungs.say: Regularization adds μ times the identity, which makes the matrix invertible

rungs.ask: Check the dimensions.
rungs.answer: Φᵀ is m × n and y is n × 1, so Φᵀy is m × 1; ΦᵀΦ + μI is m × m, so w is m × 1, one weight per basis function.
rungs.say: Dimension check: w is m by 1, one weight per basis function

ladders.trap: Switch fluently between Σᵢ, Σⱼ summation and the Φ matrix form, and keep the factor of 2 in the least squares derivative.

ladders.title: Trust region step on a saddle
ladders.freq: On the newer topic list and asked on a real recent board
ladders.figure: f(x, y) = x⁴ − 2x² + y², with the current point (0.5, 1) and a circle of radius Δ = 1 drawn around it.

rungs.ask: Find and classify the stationary points.
rungs.answer: ∇f = (4x³ − 4x, 2y) = 0 gives (0, 0) and (±1, 0); the Hessian diag(12x² − 4, 2) is indefinite at the origin, a saddle, and positive definite at (±1, 0), the minima.
rungs.say: The fourth-order term gives an indefinite Hessian at the origin, a saddle

rungs.ask: Write the trust region subproblem.
rungs.answer: Minimize the second-order model m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp subject to ‖p‖ ≤ Δ.
rungs.say: I will build a quadratic model and restrict the step to a trust region

rungs.ask: Evaluate g and B at (0.5, 1).
rungs.say: The model Hessian is indefinite here, which a trust region handles directly

rungs.ask: Find the Cauchy point.
rungs.answer: The Cauchy point minimizes the model along steepest descent inside the region: p_C = −τ(Δ/‖g‖)g with τ = min(‖g‖³/(ΔgᵀBg), 1) = min(2.72, 1) = 1, so p_C = (0.6, −0.8).
rungs.say: The Cauchy point lies along steepest descent

rungs.ask: What about the Newton step?
rungs.answer: p_N = −B⁻¹g = (−1.5, −1) heads to the stationary point of an indefinite model, a model saddle, and its length 1.80 exceeds Δ, so the method uses the boundary solution instead.
rungs.say: Newton targets the model stationary point, which here is a saddle of the model

rungs.ask: Take the Cauchy step and compute ρ.
rungs.answer: ρ = actual reduction over predicted reduction = (f(x) − f(x + p))/(m(0) − m(p)) = 1.478/2.04 ≈ 0.72.
rungs.say: ρ is actual reduction over predicted reduction

rungs.ask: Accept or reject, and what happens to Δ?
rungs.answer: ρ ≈ 0.72 exceeds the acceptance threshold, so accept; it lies between ¼ and ¾, so Δ stays at 1. The rule shrinks Δ when ρ < ¼ and expands it when ρ > ¾ with the step on the boundary.
rungs.say: Accept, and keep the radius since ρ sits between one quarter and three quarters

rungs.ask: How does this differ from line search?
rungs.answer: Line search picks a direction then a length; trust region picks a maximum length then a direction, so negative curvature is safe because the region bounds the step.
rungs.say: Trust region fixes the step size first and then chooses the direction

ladders.trap: Build the model with the second-order term, take the Cauchy point along steepest descent, and judge the step with ρ = actual over predicted reduction.

ladders.title: Electric aircraft range to a constrained corner
ladders.freq: Asked on a real recent SDO board
ladders.figure: An electric airplane with fixed battery energy E_b, and range to be maximized over weight W, wing area S and span b.

rungs.ask: Write the range.
rungs.answer: Battery mass is constant in flight, so energy equals drag times distance over efficiency: R = ηE_b/D.
rungs.say: For an electric aircraft, range equals η E_b over drag

rungs.ask: So what is the real problem?
rungs.answer: With E_b and η fixed, maximizing R is minimizing cruise drag D = qC_D0S + W²/(qπeb²).
rungs.say: Maximizing range reduces to minimizing drag

rungs.ask: Solve it unconstrained.
rungs.answer: D falls as S → 0 and as b → ∞, and W wants its lower bound, so the unconstrained answer is degenerate: zero area and infinite span.
rungs.say: The unconstrained answer is degenerate, so the constraints carry the design

rungs.ask: Which constraints fix it?
rungs.answer: A box on W at its lowest buildable weight, a stall bound S ≥ S_min, and a structural bound on aspect ratio b² ≤ AR_max S.
rungs.say: I add a structural aspect ratio limit and the stall and box bounds

rungs.ask: With the aspect ratio limit active, find the best area.
rungs.answer: Substitute b² = AR_max S: D = qC_D0S + W²/(qπeAR_max S), minimized at S* = W/(q√(πeAR_max C_D0)), where parasite drag equals induced drag.
rungs.say: With aspect ratio active, the best area makes parasite drag equal induced drag

rungs.ask: Now S_min exceeds S*. Prove the corner with KKT.
rungs.answer: Active g₁ = S_min − S ≤ 0 and g₂ = b² − AR_max S ≤ 0. The b row gives λ₂ = W²/(qπeb⁴) > 0, and the S row gives λ₁ = qC_D0 − W²/(qπeAR_max S_min²), positive exactly when S_min > S*.
rungs.say: I will set up the KKT conditions at the corner

rungs.ask: Interpret the multipliers.
rungs.answer: λ₁ is the drag cost per unit increase of S_min; λ₂ is the drag saved per unit relaxation of the aspect ratio limit, the price the structure charges the aerodynamics.
rungs.say: The multipliers are the shadow prices of stall and structure

ladders.trap: Spot the degenerate unconstrained answer (infinite span, zero area) and bring in the structural and box constraints, then confirm the corner with positive KKT multipliers.

ladders.title: Coil spring: axial, then torsional
ladders.freq: Asked two terms running: Fall 2025 axial, Spring 2026 torsional
ladders.figure: A helical spring with N coils, mean coil diameter D and wire diameter d, first pulled by an axial force F, later twisted by a moment M about its axis.

rungs.ask: Axial load. What does the wire feel?
rungs.answer: Each wire section carries a torque T = FD/2 about the wire axis (plus a small direct shear), so the wire is in torsion.
rungs.say: An axially loaded coil puts the wire in torsion

rungs.ask: Find the deflection. Name your method.
rungs.answer: Castigliano's second theorem: U = T²L_w/(2GJ) with wire length L_w = πDN and J = πd⁴/32, and δ = ∂U/∂F = 8FD³N/(Gd⁴).
rungs.say: I will use Castigliano's second theorem, δ equals ∂U over ∂F

rungs.ask: So the spring constant?
rungs.answer: k = Gd⁴/(8D³N).
rungs.say: k equals G d⁴ over 8 D³ N with D the mean coil diameter

rungs.ask: Why does a coil beat a straight bar of the same wire?
rungs.answer: The coil is a compliance amplifier: it packs a long wire, length πDN, into a short envelope and loads it through the lever arm D/2, so deflection grows as D³N while a straight bar gives only FL_w/(EA).
rungs.say: The coil packs a long wire into a small envelope and loads it through a lever arm

rungs.ask: Two of these in series, then in parallel.
rungs.answer: Series: 1/k_eq = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂, same force, deflections add. Parallel: k_eq = k₁ + k₂, same deflection, forces add.
rungs.say: Series adds compliances, parallel adds stiffnesses

rungs.ask: Now load it with a moment M about the coil axis. What does the wire feel?
rungs.answer: A moment about the coil axis bends the wire about its own cross-section axis, a bending moment M₃ of magnitude M along the whole wire, so the wire is in bending.
rungs.say: A torsional coil spring puts the wire in bending

rungs.ask: Find the rotational stiffness.
rungs.answer: U = M²L_w/(2EI) with I = πd⁴/64, θ = ∂U/∂M = 64MDN/(Ed⁴), so k_θ = Ed⁴/(64DN).
rungs.say: Same energy method, now with EI and I = πd⁴/64

rungs.ask: Limiting case check.
rungs.answer: Both stiffnesses fall as N rises, since more coils means a longer wire, and rise steeply with wire diameter as d⁴.
rungs.say: Check: more coils makes it softer, thicker wire makes it stiffer with d⁴

ladders.trap: An axial force puts the wire in torsion (use GJ, J = πd⁴/32); a moment about the coil axis puts the wire in bending (use EI, I = πd⁴/64).

ladders.title: Bulk modulus of a particle composite
ladders.figure: A cube under uniform pressure p on every face, then the same cube redrawn as matrix A filled with particles of B at volume fraction f.

rungs.ask: Define the bulk modulus.
rungs.answer: K = −V dp/dV, so under pressure p the volumetric strain is ΔV/V = −p/K.
rungs.say: Bulk modulus relates pressure to volumetric strain

rungs.ask: What does it mean physically?
rungs.answer: K measures resistance to change of volume with shape held fixed; a large K means a nearly incompressible solid.
rungs.say: It is the stiffness against volume change at fixed shape

rungs.ask: Derive it for an isotropic linear elastic solid.
rungs.answer: Under σ = −pI each normal strain is −p(1 − 2ν)/E, so ε_kk = −3p(1 − 2ν)/E and K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) = λ + 2μ/3.
rungs.say: I apply a hydrostatic stress and sum the three normal strains

rungs.ask: What happens as ν goes to one half?
rungs.answer: K → ∞, the incompressible limit, while the shear modulus stays finite.
rungs.say: At ν equals one half the solid becomes incompressible

rungs.ask: Now the composite. Build an estimate.
rungs.answer: Assume the same pressure p in every phase. Volume changes add by volume fraction: ΔV/V = −p[(1 − f)/K_A + f/K_B], so 1/K_eff = (1 − f)/K_A + f/K_B.
rungs.say: I assume uniform pressure in both phases and add the volume changes

rungs.ask: What did that assumption ignore, and which bound is it?
rungs.answer: Uniform stress ignores the interface shear that keeps the phases compatible, which is the Reuss (series) estimate, the lower bound on K_eff; uniform strain gives the Voigt upper bound K = (1 − f)K_A + fK_B.
rungs.say: Uniform stress is the Reuss lower bound, uniform strain is the Voigt upper bound

rungs.ask: Limit check: rigid particles.
rungs.answer: K_B → ∞ gives K_eff = K_A/(1 − f), and f = 0 recovers K_A.
rungs.say: Check the limits f equals zero and rigid particles

ladders.trap: State that the uniform pressure (series) estimate is the Reuss lower bound on K_eff, with the uniform strain Voigt estimate as the upper bound.

ladders.title: Rope angle for an all-compressive beam
ladders.figure: A horizontal beam of length L and rectangular depth h, pinned to a wall at its left end, its right end held up by a rope running back to the wall at angle α above the beam, under a uniform load w.

rungs.ask: Free body diagram. Find the rope tension.
rungs.answer: Moments about the pin: T sinα · L = wL²/2, so T = wL/(2 sinα), and T must come out as tension because a rope only pulls.
rungs.say: A rope carries tension only, so I draw T pulling and check its sign

rungs.ask: What does the rope do to the beam besides hold it up?
rungs.answer: Its horizontal component T cosα = wL/(2 tanα) pushes the beam into the wall, a uniform axial compression N.
rungs.say: The rope's horizontal component puts the beam in axial compression

rungs.ask: Bending moment?
rungs.answer: Vertical reactions are wL/2 at each end, so the beam bends like a simply supported span with M_max = wL²/8 at midspan, tension on the bottom fibre.
rungs.say: Maximum moment is wL² over 8 at midspan with the bottom fibre in tension

rungs.ask: Write the stress at the bottom fibre.
rungs.answer: σ_bottom = −N/A + M c/I with c = h/2; the axial term shifts the neutral axis toward the tension side.
rungs.say: I superpose axial and bending stress

rungs.ask: Find the α that makes the whole section compressive.
rungs.answer: Set σ_bottom ≤ 0 at midspan, which moves the neutral axis to the extreme fibre: N/A ≥ M_max c/I gives tanα ≤ 4I/(ALc) = 2h/(3L) for a rectangle.
rungs.say: I shift the neutral axis to the extreme fibre

rungs.ask: Explain that with the kern.
rungs.answer: The section stays compressive when the load eccentricity e = M/N is within the kern, h/6 for a rectangle: (L tanα)/4 ≤ h/6 gives the same tanα ≤ 2h/(3L).
rungs.say: Equivalent statement: the eccentricity M over N stays inside the kern, h over 6

rungs.ask: A shallower rope gives more compression. What else must you check?
rungs.answer: The beam is now a column: check N ≤ π²EI/L² for the pinned-pinned span, and note the beam-column amplification of the moment as N approaches that load.
rungs.say: With large compression I check buckling and beam-column amplification

ladders.trap: Draw the rope force as tension (a rope only pulls), then shift the neutral axis to the extreme fibre to get tanα ≤ 2h/(3L), and check column buckling under the added compression.

ladders.title: Inflating an incompressible balloon
ladders.figure: A thin spherical membrane of initial radius R₀ and thickness t₀, made of an incompressible neo-Hookean rubber, inflated by internal pressure P to radius R.

rungs.ask: Write the stretches.
rungs.answer: λ_θ = λ_φ = λ = R/R₀ and λ_R = t/t₀; incompressibility λ_Rλ_θλ_φ = 1 gives λ_R = λ⁻².
rungs.say: Incompressibility ties thickness stretch to the hoop stretches

rungs.ask: Write the Cauchy stress for the neo-Hookean solid.
rungs.answer: σ = −pI + μB with B = FFᵀ, so σ_θθ = −p + μλ² and σ_rr = −p + μλ⁻⁴, where p is the pressure multiplier from incompressibility.
rungs.say: p is a Lagrange multiplier enforcing incompressibility

rungs.ask: How do you find p?
rungs.answer: The membrane is thin, so the radial stress is small compared with the hoop stress: σ_rr = 0 gives p = μλ⁻⁴ and σ_θθ = μ(λ² − λ⁻⁴).
rungs.say: I fix the multiplier from σ_rr equals zero through the thin wall

rungs.ask: Equilibrium. Find P as a function of λ.
rungs.answer: Cut the sphere in half: PπR² = σ_θθ·2πRt, so P = 2σ_θθt/R = 2μ(t₀/R₀)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷).
rungs.say: Half-sphere equilibrium gives P equals 2σt over R in the current geometry

rungs.ask: Small strain check.
rungs.answer: With λ = 1 + ε, P ≈ 12μεt₀/R₀, matching linear thin-sphere theory with E = 3μ and ν = ½.
rungs.say: The small strain limit recovers linear theory

rungs.ask: Why is a balloon hard to start and then easier?
rungs.answer: dP/dλ = 0 gives λ⁶ = 7, so the pressure peaks at λ = 7^(1/6) ≈ 1.38 with P_max ≈ 1.24μt₀/R₀ and then falls as the wall thins.
rungs.say: The pressure curve has a limit point at λ equal to 7 to the one sixth

rungs.ask: What kind of instability is that?
rungs.answer: A limit point: under controlled pressure the balloon snaps through to a much larger radius at P_max; under controlled volume it passes smoothly.
rungs.say: This is a limit point, so under pressure control it snaps through

ladders.trap: Use current geometry, t = t₀λ⁻² and R = R₀λ, in the equilibrium P = 2σt/R, and find the multiplier p from σ_rr = 0.

ladders.title: Two-bar spring column, start to finish
ladders.freq: This chair's rigid-bar ladder (Π, equilibrium, P_cr, post-buckling, imperfections) recycled its figure 2021, 2023, 2026; zero second variation asked Fall 2025
ladders.figure: Two rigid bars of length L stacked vertically, a rotational spring C at the base pin, a second spring C at the middle hinge, and a vertical dead load P at the free top.

rungs.ask: Set up the total potential with every term.
rungs.answer: Angles θ₁, θ₂ from the vertical: Π = ½Cθ₁² + ½C(θ₂ − θ₁)² − PL(2 − cosθ₁ − cosθ₂).
rungs.say: The middle spring sees the relative angle, ½C(θ₂ − θ₁)²

rungs.ask: Equilibrium.
rungs.answer: ∂Π/∂θ₁ = Cθ₁ − C(θ₂ − θ₁) − PL sinθ₁ = 0 and ∂Π/∂θ₂ = C(θ₂ − θ₁) − PL sinθ₂ = 0; θ₁ = θ₂ = 0 is the trivial path for every P.
rungs.say: Stationary total potential gives equilibrium

rungs.ask: Linearize and find P_cr.
rungs.answer: The Hessian at zero is [[2C − PL, −C], [−C, C − PL]]; det = 0 gives (PL)² − 3C(PL) + C² = 0, so P_cr = (3 − √5)C/(2L) ≈ 0.382C/L.
rungs.say: I set the determinant of the second variation matrix to zero

rungs.ask: Mode shape?
rungs.answer: θ₂/θ₁ = (1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618, both bars leaning the same way with the top bar leaning more.
rungs.say: The buckling mode is the null vector at P_cr

rungs.ask: Stability of the trivial path.
rungs.answer: Below P_cr the Hessian is positive definite, so the straight column is stable; above P_cr it has a negative eigenvalue and the straight column is unstable.
rungs.say: Positive definite second variation means stable

rungs.ask: At P_cr the second variation is zero along the mode. Is it stable?
rungs.answer: The second-order test is inconclusive there, so go to higher order: the cubic terms vanish by symmetry and the quartic term +(PL/24)(θ₁⁴ + θ₂⁴) is positive, so the critical point is stable.
rungs.say: Zero second variation is inconclusive, so I go to higher-order terms

rungs.ask: Post-buckling. Expand to the right order.
rungs.answer: Use cosθ ≈ 1 − θ²/2 + θ⁴/24 and keep every term to θ⁴; the quadratic terms locate P_cr and the quartic terms give P rising with amplitude, P ≈ P_cr(1 + c a²) with c > 0.
rungs.say: The quadratic term locates P_cr and the quartic term decides post-buckling

rungs.ask: Classify the bifurcation.
rungs.answer: Rising load after buckling with a symmetric path is a stable symmetric bifurcation; a falling path would be unstable symmetric, and a linear term in a would be asymmetric.
rungs.say: Rising post-buckling path: stable symmetric bifurcation

rungs.ask: Add a small initial tilt. Imperfection sensitive?
rungs.answer: Stable symmetric is imperfection insensitive: the deflection grows smoothly as P approaches P_cr and the load can rise past it. Unstable symmetric systems lose load capacity with the two-thirds power of the imperfection.
rungs.say: Stable symmetric is imperfection insensitive; the two-thirds power law belongs to unstable symmetric

ladders.trap: When d²Π = 0 at the critical point, state that the second-order test is inconclusive and examine the cubic and quartic terms, keeping every term of the expansion to θ⁴.

ladders.title: Thin-walled tube that turns out thick
ladders.freq: This chair's signature trap: the required t comes out as D/4
ladders.figure: A beam whose circular cross section of diameter D has a concentric hole, drawn as a thin ring, carrying a torque T with an allowable shear stress τ_allow and the instruction: size the wall.

rungs.ask: Which theory do you use?
rungs.answer: Thin-walled closed section torsion (Bredt): shear flow q = T/(2A), shear stress τ = q/t, with A the area enclosed by the mid-wall line.
rungs.say: I will assume a thin wall and use Bredt's formula, q equals T over 2A

rungs.ask: State the assumption you just made.
rungs.answer: Thin wall means t is small compared with the radius, typically t/R ≤ 1/10, so the shear stress is uniform through the thickness.
rungs.say: My assumption is t much smaller than R, uniform stress through the wall

rungs.ask: Size it with T = πD³τ_allow/8.
rungs.answer: t = T/(2Aτ_allow) with A = πD²/4, so t = 2T/(πD²τ_allow) = D/4.
rungs.say: I write the final asked-for quantity, t equals D over 4

rungs.ask: Is that a good answer?
rungs.answer: t = D/4 gives t/R = ½, which violates the thin-wall assumption the formula rests on, so the result is invalid and the section needs thick-wall analysis.
rungs.say: Stop: t equals D over 4 violates my thin-wall assumption

rungs.ask: Redo it properly.
rungs.answer: Use exact circular-shaft torsion: τ_max = Tr_o/J with J = π(r_o⁴ − r_i⁴)/2, and solve for the inner radius that keeps τ_max at τ_allow.
rungs.say: For a thick tube I use τ equals T r over J with the polar J

rungs.ask: Now cut a slit along the full length. What happens to the stiffness?
rungs.answer: The section becomes open: J_open = (1/3)st³ with s = 2πR, versus J_closed = 4A²t/s = 2πR³t, a ratio J_closed/J_open = 3R²/t², a huge loss for a thin wall.
rungs.say: A slit turns a closed cell into an open section, J drops to one third s t³

rungs.ask: Same tube in bending. Which section property?
rungs.answer: Bending uses I = π(r_o⁴ − r_i⁴)/4, half the polar J, and the thin-wall form I ≈ πR³t.
rungs.say: Bending uses I, torsion uses the polar J equal to 2I for a circle

ladders.trap: When the sized wall comes out t = D/4, stop and say the thin-wall assumption is violated, then switch to thick-wall torsion with J = π(r_o⁴ − r_i⁴)/2.

ladders.title: Strut-braced wing as a spring
ladders.freq: Replacing a member with an equivalent spring asked 2020 and 2021
ladders.figure: A cantilever wing beam of bending stiffness EI under a tip load P, braced by a strut of axial stiffness EA and length L_s attached at distance a from the root at angle β to the wing.

rungs.ask: What kind of member is the strut?
rungs.answer: Pinned at both ends and loaded only at its ends, it is a two-force member carrying axial force only.
rungs.say: The strut is a two-force member, so it carries axial load

rungs.ask: Replace it with a spring.
rungs.answer: Axial stiffness k_s = EA/L_s; its stiffness against vertical motion of the wing at the attachment is k_v = (EA/L_s)sin²β.
rungs.say: I replace the strut with an axial spring and project it twice, giving sin²β

rungs.ask: Now the wing is indeterminate. Set it up.
rungs.answer: Release the strut reaction R and use compatibility: wing deflection at a under P minus that under R equals R/k_v.
rungs.say: One redundant, so I use compatibility with the spring

rungs.ask: Write the compatibility equation.
rungs.answer: P(a²/(6EI))(3L − a) − Ra³/(3EI) = R/k_v, so R = P(a²(3L − a)/(6EI))/(a³/(3EI) + 1/k_v).
rungs.say: For the redundant, beam flexibility and spring flexibility add

rungs.ask: Check the limits.
rungs.answer: k_v → ∞ gives the rigid prop reaction; k_v → 0 gives R = 0 and the plain cantilever.
rungs.say: Check: infinite spring stiffness gives a rigid support, zero gives the free cantilever

rungs.ask: The root is a real fitting, slightly flexible. Model it.
rungs.answer: Replace the clamp by a linear spring for vertical slip and a rotational spring for root rotation, both together, and add ½k_ru² + ½k_θφ² to the energy.
rungs.say: A real support may need both a linear and a rotational spring

rungs.ask: Series or parallel?
rungs.answer: Elements sharing the same force act in series (compliances add); elements sharing the same displacement act in parallel (stiffnesses add); the strut and the wing beam at the attachment share displacement, so they act in parallel there.
rungs.say: Same force means series, same displacement means parallel

ladders.trap: Project the strut stiffness onto the wing deflection direction twice, k_v = (EA/L_s)sin²β, and check both spring limits.

ladders.title: Rayleigh-Ritz: trial functions and springs
ladders.freq: Change-the-trial-function question asked in two different years
ladders.figure: A cantilever of length L and stiffness EI with a tip load P, later with a spring k under the tip, later with the clamp replaced by a rotational spring.

rungs.ask: Set up the Ritz approximation.
rungs.answer: Π = ∫₀ᴸ ½EI(w″)² dx − Pw(L), with a trial function that satisfies the kinematic boundary conditions w(0) = 0 and w′(0) = 0.
rungs.say: I will use Rayleigh-Ritz on the total potential energy, with the load potential entering with a minus sign

rungs.ask: Use w = a x².
rungs.answer: Π = 2EIL a² − PL²a, ∂Π/∂a = 0 gives a = PL/(4EI) and tip deflection PL³/(4EI).
rungs.say: Stationarity with respect to each Ritz coefficient

rungs.ask: Compare with exact.
rungs.answer: Exact is PL³/(3EI). Ritz gives a stiffer structure, so the approximate deflection is smaller and Π is an upper bound on the true minimum.
rungs.say: Ritz is stiffer than exact, so it underestimates deflection here

rungs.ask: Change the trial function to a x² + b x³.
rungs.answer: Two equations in a and b give tip deflection PL³/(3EI), the exact answer, because the exact cubic lies in the trial space.
rungs.say: Adding the cubic puts the exact solution in the trial space

rungs.ask: Put a spring k under the tip.
rungs.answer: Add ½k w(L)² to Π. With w = a x², tip deflection becomes PL³/(4EI + kL³).
rungs.say: The spring adds its strain energy to Π

rungs.ask: Does the trial function need to change for the spring?
rungs.answer: The spring support is a natural boundary condition, so the trial function only needs the kinematic conditions; the energy term enforces the force balance.
rungs.say: Spring supports are natural boundary conditions

rungs.ask: Replace the clamp with a rotational spring C.
rungs.answer: Now w(0) = 0 is the only kinematic condition, so the trial needs a linear term, w = a₁x + a₂x² + ..., and Π gains ½C(w′(0))².
rungs.say: Release the kinematic condition, enrich the trial function, add the spring energy

ladders.trap: Make the trial function satisfy the kinematic boundary conditions, treat spring supports as natural boundary conditions through their energy, and enter the load potential with a minus sign.

ladders.title: Finite simple shear of an infinite slab
ladders.figure: A slab of thickness h, infinitely long in x₁ and x₃, with its top face slid by γh in x₁ relative to its bottom face.

rungs.ask: Write the motion and F.
rungs.answer: x₁ = X₁ + γX₂, x₂ = X₂, x₃ = X₃, so F = [[1, γ, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]] and det F = 1, isochoric.
rungs.say: Simple shear is isochoric, det F equals 1

rungs.ask: Left Cauchy-Green tensor?
rungs.say: B equals F F transpose

rungs.ask: Stress for an incompressible neo-Hookean solid.
rungs.answer: σ = −pI + μB, so σ₁₂ = μγ, σ₁₁ = −p + μ(1 + γ²), σ₂₂ = −p + μ, σ₃₃ = −p + μ.
rungs.say: I use σ equals minus p I plus μ B

rungs.ask: How do you find p?
rungs.answer: The loading plates apply shear traction only, so the normal traction on the faces normal to x₂ is zero: σ₂₂ = 0 gives p = μ, so σ₁₁ = μγ² and σ₃₃ = 0.
rungs.say: I find p from the normal traction condition on the sheared faces

rungs.ask: Physical meaning of τ/G?
rungs.answer: τ/G = σ₁₂/μ = γ, the amount of shear, the tangent of the angle through which an initially vertical material line tilts.
rungs.say: τ over G is the amount of shear, the tangent of the shear angle

rungs.ask: Why does an axial normal stress appear?
rungs.answer: Maintaining finite simple shear needs a normal stress difference σ₁₁ − σ₂₂ = μγ², a second-order effect in γ (the Poynting effect) that small strain theory drops.
rungs.say: The normal stress is second order in γ, a finite deformation effect

rungs.ask: Check the small strain limit.
rungs.answer: As γ → 0, σ₁₂ = μγ recovers linear shear τ = Gγ, and the normal stresses of order γ² vanish faster.
rungs.say: Small strain recovers τ equals G γ

ladders.trap: Find the pressure multiplier p from the zero normal traction on the faces normal to x₂ (they carry shear only), then read off the normal stress σ₁₁ − σ₂₂ = μγ² as the second-order finite shear effect.
